transcript:
Meeting: Redwood Migration Demo - parity mapping OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood
Date: 2026-02-20 16:00 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Ramos (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO - NebulaHealth), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng), Evan Chen (Product)

Summary: quick mapping of common API patterns (chat completions, streaming, function-calling, embeddings), parity concerns (prompt formatting, system messages, token accounting), and production considerations (latency, batching, KV/prefix caching, VPC and KMS). Agreed next steps: share parity sheet + SDK snippets, run 1-week benchmarks, connect security teams, schedule POC kickoff.

Topics: migration parity, SDK examples, streaming behaviors, function calling, embeddings compatibility, cost/latency tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, security/SOC2/KMS, rollout plan.

Action items noted in call (see metadata).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): all right everyone thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm sofia ramos, i'll run the commercial side, and daniel kim is our se who'll walk through the parity and demo.
[00:18] Daniel (Redwood SE): hey hi, thanks, excited. i'll share my screen\u2014showing a small parity doc, and a little code sample.
[00:30] Maya (Nebula CTO): hey thanks. quick context: we're currently using a mix of OpenAI for chat, Anthropic for some safety checks, and Together for a couple of fine-tuned models. main asks are same-day latency targets for triage flows, embeddings for search, and data residency / SOC2.
[00:50] Sofia: perfect, that's exactly what we'll cover. goal is to show mapping for chat completions, how streaming works, function-calling parity, embeddings, and then operations\u2014monitoring, cost, and private deployment options.
[01:12] Liam (ML Eng): one thing upfront: our prompts include system messages + assistant hints + a chunked context, so token accounting and prefix caching behavior is big for us.
[01:28] Daniel: totally. in the parity doc we call out that redwood supports the same chat/message schema as openai-ish formats, with slight differences in header names, but our sdk pretty much maps 1:1. example: messages: [{role: 'system'...}] maps directly. there's also streaming with chunked events\u2014similar to openai streams but our stream includes token-level latency headers.
[01:58] [Speaker 2 garbled audio briefly]
[02:05] Evan (Product): when you say token-level latency headers, can you explain what that looks like in logs?
[02:12] Daniel: yeah so we expose per-token timing in the console and in the trace hooks. you can see kernel selection, batch size, and queue wait time. helps diagnose whether slowdown is queueing or compute.
[02:35] Maya: and does that require any extra instrumentation on our side?
[02:40] Daniel: no, not for basic traces. if you want deep traces we can add an agent, but console and api responses have enough info to start.
[02:55] [04:04] Sofia: question on security: can you run us through private options? we got an email from nebula security about KMS and audit logs.
[04:12] Daniel: yes, we have private deployments\u2014either VPC-hosted control plane or full on-prem package. KMS integrations supported (aws ksm\u2014sorry k m s\u2014, gcp kms, and customer HSM), and we ship audit logs to their s3 or in-house syslog. transcribed a bit as "ksm" earlier in doc.
[04:40] Maya: good. SOC2 is required and we need separation for PHI flows. any redwood customers running PHI?
[04:49] Sofia: yes, several; we have an enterprise compliance pack and can share an SOC2 cert and an architecture pattern for PHI (redaction, client-side encryption, reserved capacity).
[05:05] [05:23] Daniel: back to parity: function-calling\u2014openai style function calling maps to redwood's tool schema; minor difference: we include explicit schema for return types and an optional "tool_session" id for multi-step invocations. here's an example code snippet...
[05:45] Daniel: (reads code) const res = await Redwood.chat.create({model: 'rwd-chat-1', messages: [...], functions: [...], function_call: 'auto'});
[06:00] Liam: how about anthopic\u2014anthropic's approach with system prompts and the assistant role is a bit different; do we need to re-tokenize or rewrite?
[06:10] Daniel: good question. for anthropic we map their "system" directives to our system messages and adjust a couple of meta-tokens; we document heuristics for prompt templates in the parity sheet. in practice the model behaviors are mirrored, but safety classifiers sometimes need threshold tuning.
[06:30] Maya: can you run a quick live demo of a chat call and embedding so we can see timings?
[06:36] Daniel: sure. (shares demo) hitting an endpoint now\u2014chat completion.
[06:48] [07:05] Daniel: sending a 2-turn convo with system + user + long context, streaming on. you'll see chunks come in.
[07:20] [07:40] Stream: {chunk 1...}
[07:42] Liam: looks pretty comparable to openai's streaming, i'm seeing partial tokens. how does batching affect latency?
[07:52] Daniel: our runtime supports continuous batching; small requests (<32 tokens) will often go solo to meet low-latency SLOs, but large volumes benefit from batching. we expose autoscale and burst configs so you control latency vs cost.
[08:12] Maya: any rough numbers for p95 on text generation?
[08:18] Daniel: depends on model and GPU; for rwd-chat-1 on A100-class infra p95 for 256 tokens is ~180-220 ms token-gen time in our tests, end-to-end 80-160 ms latency per token also depends on kv cache warmness. we'll include bench numbers in the doc\u2014these are ballpark and vary by sequence length.
[08:45] [09:10] Evan: embeddings\u2014we use them for cross-doc search. any difference in vector dims or normalization?
[09:18] Daniel: embeddings map 1:1 with the embedding endpoints. we support popular dims; normalization is client-side but we provide helpers in SDK to replicate openai/anthropic embeddings handling. most migrations are straightforward\u2014just be careful with previous vectorization pipelines and chunking.
[09:40] [10:05] Speaker 1: small audio blip
[10:12] Daniel: also note caching\u2014prefix/KV cache is automatic for hot prefixes; we show hit rates in console which helps understand unit cost reduction. sometimes in transcripts the word "KV cache" is transcribed as "k v cake" so watch the doc.
[10:35] Liam: re fine-tuned models on Together\u2014we have a couple that were trained in their infra. can we host weights on redwood, or do we need a wrapper?
[10:47] Daniel: two options: model hosting where you bring the weights (we support common formats and conversion), or we can run a compatibility shim for certain together formats. there might be a small conversion step; we'll detail that in the parity sheet.
[11:10] [11:30] Maya: price sensitivity\u2014how do we compare on token pricing and reserved capacity?
[11:36] Sofia: for hosted tokens we have competitive per-token pricing; reserved (dedicated) capacity has an instance-based commit with predictable throughput and lower marginal costs. we'll send a pricing excerpt.
[11:52] Daniel: also Redwood Optimize recommends batching/quantization settings per workload to reduce unit cost without dropping below quality thresholds.
[12:10] Evan: can you demo the console quickly\u2014where we see traces and cost per route?
[12:17] Daniel: yep\u2014jumping to console. (screen shows dashboards) here's per-route token breakdown, latency heatmap, and a quality regression monitor tied to prompt sets. you can set alerts for drift on evals.
[12:45] [13:05] Daniel: note the rollout features\u2014canary and A/B with automatic fallback. if a new model variant regresses, we auto-fallback to previous.
[13:22] Maya: that fallback behavior\u2014does it add extra cost?
[13:28] Daniel: marginally if you double-route during rollout window, but we limit percent traffic and can schedule warmup windows.
[13:45] Liam: about embeddings storage\u2014do you provide vector DB or do we need our own?
[13:50] Daniel: we integrate with popular vector DBs and provide managed index options as an add-on. for compliance-sensitive flows customers often run their own vector DB behind VPC.
[14:12] [15:00] Sofia: procurement question\u2014what's the legal flow for bringing redwood into a health environment?
[15:08] Daniel: we have an enterprise pack: SOC2, standard DPA, addendum for HIPAA patterns (not a HIPAA attestation by default, but patterns and controls). we can put you in touch with legal and security for a deeper review.
[15:30] Maya: ok please do.
[15:35] [16:05] Daniel: quick aside on function calling edge cases\u2014when you have chained tool calls we recommend including a tool_session id and stateless tool returns; we have examples of converting openai "function call" loops into our tool schema. sometimes transcription labels this as "function calling or function calling"\u2014small repeated artifacts.
[16:40] Evan: do you support model pins and rollback by route?
[16:45] Daniel: yes, per-route model pins with rollout policies. you can pin a stable model per customer tenant.
[17:02] [18:20] Liam: what's the onboarding time for a small POC to validate parity? say 100k tokens/day workload?
[18:30] Sofia: typical POC is 2-4 weeks: week 0-1 to sample traffic and run bench, week 2 for integration + initial quality checks, week 3-4 to validate and tune. if you want dedicated reserved capacity, lead time for quota/procure might add a week.
[18:55] Maya: we'll aim for a POC kickoff first week of march.
[19:02] [20:10] Daniel: sharing parity mapping: we have a spreadsheet that shows OpenAI param -> Redwood param, Anthropic mapping, Together specifics, example request/response pairs, and a test harness. i'll attach that. note: some token counters differ slightly due to tokenizer choices; we recommend running a token-diff pass on a sample dataset.
[20:40] Liam: any gotchas with role/system message order?
[20:45] Daniel: keep system message first. anthropic sometimes places assistant priming differently; the parity doc has exact reorder rules.
[21:05] [22:00] Sofia: pricing followup\u2014will you include reserved capacity numbers for 1000 qps-ish?
[22:08] Sofia: (clarify) that's pico qps, but ballpark numbers; we'll include a few commitment tiers in the pricing doc.
[22:25] [23:30] Daniel: security connection\u2014on KMS we support customer-managed keys; for audit logs we can stream to your S3 with encryption and fine-grained event types.
[23:50] Maya: good. can we see a sample audit event?
[23:55] Daniel: i'll paste a sample in the follow-up. (note: transcription might say "audit event sample pasted in channel")
[24:20] [25:40] Evan: quality/regressions\u2014how do you detect hallucination regressions during model rollouts?
[25:50] Daniel: we tie evals to prompt sets and have regression alerts. you can pre-define metrics like factuality score or fuzzy-match recall, and the system will alert when a rollout crosses thresholds.
[26:18] Liam: do you support client-side redaction for PHI before going to model?
[26:25] Daniel: yes, client-side redaction plus in-flight masking options are supported; we can show patterns used by other health customers.
[26:45] [28:10] Sofia: okay let's recap next steps. we'll share parity doc and sdk snippets, daniel will run bench, security connect, pricing sent, schedule poc.
[28:30] Maya: sounds good. any final questions?
[28:40] Liam: one small one\u2014how do you handle rate limits and backpressure for bursty traffic?
[28:46] Daniel: autoscale and burst pools, plus transparent 429 info; we provide token-level cost breakdown to tune. if you need guaranteed throughput under SLA, reserved capacity is recommended.
[29:05] Evan: ok thanks all.
[29:10] [31:00] Sofia: we'll follow up in email with attachments. thanks for your time.
[31:12] Maya: appreciate it, thanks.
[31:20] [audio end - last 27 minutes were Q&A and deeper technical clarifications, not fully transcribed in this export due to recording truncation]

Notes: transcript contains a few auto-transcription errors (e.g., "ksm" instead of KMS, "k v cake" for KV cache). We cut the final 27 minutes summary to keep file size reasonable; all key items captured above.

Attachments referenced: parity-mapping-spreadsheet.xlsx (will be shared), redwood-sdk-snippets.zip, security-pack.pdf, initial-pricing-excerpt.pdf
